title: Dealing with Contention
subtitle: What to do when many users race to change the same thing — locks, atomic updates, optimistic concurrency, and serialising work.
seoTitle: Design Dealing with Contention | System Design Interview Breakdown
description: What to do when many users race to change the same thing — locks, atomic updates, optimistic concurrency, and serialising work.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: Two people click "Book" on the last concert seat. A thousand bidders hit the same auction in its final second. Ten thousand buyers fight over a flash-sale inventory counter. **Contention** is when concurrent operations compete to modify the same piece of data — and getting it wrong means double bookings, oversold stock and lost updates.

blocks.code:
remaining = SELECT remaining FROM inventory WHERE id = 1   -- both read 1
if remaining > 0:
    UPDATE inventory SET remaining = remaining - 1           -- both write 0
    create_order()                                            -- two orders!

blocks.text: Each request is correct on its own. Interleaved, they both pass the check before either writes. Any time your logic reads a value, decides, and then writes, you have a race unless something makes the sequence atomic.

approach.text: Lock the row before reading it so others wait: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction, then check and write, then commit to release the lock.

challenges.text: Correct and easy to reason about, but contenders queue on the lock. Never hold a database lock across user think-time (like a checkout page) — use a reservation with a TTL instead.

approach.text: Let the database check and write in one statement:
No lock is held across round trips, and losers fail fast.

challenges.text: Only works when the whole decision fits in a single conditional statement.

approach.text: Read the row with a `version` column, compute the change, then `UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = :readVersion`. If zero rows changed, someone else won — re-read and retry.

challenges.text: Excellent when conflicts are rare. Under heavy contention, retries pile up and waste work.

approach.text: When the contended resource spans systems, or you need to hold it for minutes (a seat during checkout), acquire a lock in Redis with `SET key owner NX EX 600`. The TTL releases it automatically if the user abandons.

challenges.text: Lock-service failover can grant a lock twice; protect critical writes with **fencing tokens** (a monotonically increasing number checked by the database) and keep the database constraint as the final safety net.

approach.text: Route all operations for one entity to one place — a queue partition keyed by entity ID, or an actor/owner process — which handles them one at a time. No concurrent writers means no race.

challenges.text: Throughput per entity is bounded by one consumer, and you need to handle ownership changes safely.

items: [Online Auction](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/online-auction) — accepting only bids higher than the current max.
[Uber](/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/uber) — not offering one driver two rides at once.

blocks.text: How do you handle extreme contention on one item?

Filter demand before it reaches the hot row: a waiting room or queue admits requests at a sustainable rate, an in-memory atomic counter (Redis `DECR`) absorbs the burst, and the database records the outcome asynchronously. You can also split the resource into shards (ten counters of 100 units each) to spread the load.
When a single operation spans several databases, there is no shared transaction. Use a saga with compensating actions, or reserve resources with TTLs in each service and confirm them in a final step.
Why keep a database constraint if you already lock?
Locks can fail in subtle ways (expired TTLs, failovers). A unique constraint or a `CHECK (remaining >= 0)` is cheap insurance that turns a silent data bug into a loud error.

Spot the read-check-write. Prefer making the decision atomic in the database; reach for optimistic concurrency when conflicts are rare, distributed locks with TTLs when holding resources across time or systems, and a single owner when one entity is extremely hot.

quiz.question: What is the core bug behind most contention problems?
quiz.explanation: Concurrent requests read the same state before any of them writes, so all pass the check.

quiz.question: When is optimistic concurrency control a good fit?
quiz.explanation: Version checks avoid locks; retries are cheap only if conflicts are uncommon.

quiz.question: Why add a TTL to a distributed lock?
options: So it is released automatically if the holder crashes or abandons
quiz.explanation: Without a TTL a crashed holder could block the resource forever.

quiz.question: What do fencing tokens protect against?
options: A stale lock holder writing after its lock was granted to someone else
quiz.explanation: The storage layer rejects writes carrying an older token than the latest it has seen.
